channel.title: The New Yorker — Reporting
channel.description: Latest reporting from The New Yorker

item.title: Cinema of Wayward Souls
item.description: The director Lee Chang-dong excavates the traumas of contemporary Korean history in starkly personal terms.

item.title: We’re Learning to Live with Waymos. It’s Going Weird
item.description: A view from the back seat.

item.title: How the D.S.A. Learned to Love Elections
item.description: Members of the Democratic Socialists of America believe deeply in the possibility of a class revolution. Meanwhile, they’re running for office—and winning.

item.title: Computer Chips Are the Most Magnificent Things Humanity Has Ever Made
item.description: They power our phones, cars, dishwashers—and the A.I. systems that prop up the economy. They’re also at the heart of fierce geopolitical rivalry.

item.title: The New Age of Reading
item.description: Alarm about declining interest in books is perpetual. But, as bookselling reaches unexpected heights, James Daunt, the chief executive of Barnes & Noble, thinks a different future is at hand.

item.title: The Danger of Getting Too Close to a Source
item.description: Richard Darman was my source in the Reagan and Bush Administrations—and my best friend.

item.title: The State Officials Defending the Midterms from the President
item.description: Donald Trump has tried to purge voter rolls nationwide. Deidre Henderson, the Republican lieutenant governor of Utah, is among the chief election officers standing in his way.

item.title: Charles Kushner and the MAGA Ambassador’s Playbook
item.description: Since taking up his post in Paris, Kushner has become known for lobbing provocations onto France’s domestic scene at sensitive moments. As he put it, “Nobody has the courage to say what I say.”

item.title: How Jim Morrison Surmounted Tragedy and Skied Down Everest
item.description: The mountaineer and his partner, Hilaree Nelson, planned a first-ever descent. After her death, he pushed on.

item.title: Did an Alternative-Medicine Guru Accidentally Kill Patients?
item.description: In Switzerland, Thomas Rau offers treatments that many conventional doctors would question. Now he’s accused of lethally negligent care.
